items.stem: An owner sees that noodles and sardines share 6 of 12 receipts. She puts them on the same shelf. What does the pattern tell her?

options.text: Buying noodles makes people want sardines.
options.feedback: Receipts show what was bought together. They do not show that one purchase causes the other.

options.text: Half the receipts is too few to act on.
options.feedback: Half of all receipts is a large share. A pair on 3 of 12 receipts would be a weaker case.

options.text: Shoppers often buy the two together, so a shared shelf suits them.
options.feedback: A pair on half the receipts is common enough to act on.

options.text: Both items sell out every day.
options.feedback: The count covers pairs on one receipt. It says nothing about daily totals.

items.stem: A rider's message is SSSLSSSLSSSL. A teammate shortens it to "SSSL, repeat 3 times." A rider follows the short version and goes straight twice, then turns left. What went wrong?

options.text: The message has no repeat, so it cannot be shortened.
options.feedback: SSSL repeats three times, so the shortening is valid.

options.text: The block should have been 6 symbols long.
options.feedback: A block of 6 does not rebuild the message. SSSLSS and SLSSSL differ.

options.text: The short version is longer than the original.
options.feedback: The short version has 5 symbols and the original has 12.

options.text: The rider dropped one S from the block, so the block became SSL.
options.feedback: SSSL means straight three times, then left. Two straights and a left is a different block.

items.stem: Saturdays sold 60 and 58 cups in weeks 1 and 3, and 20 cups in week 2. Every other day is close to its twin in the other weeks. What should the owner do before changing next week's order?

options.text: Order only 20 cups on Saturdays from now on.
options.feedback: One low Saturday does not replace two high ones.

options.text: Find out what happened that Saturday, such as a typhoon.
options.feedback: One odd day is a signal to ask why. The reason decides whether next week needs a change.

options.text: Ignore the day, because an outlier is always an error.
options.feedback: An outlier can be an error or a real event. Check it before dropping it.

options.text: Order the average of the three Saturdays, 46 cups.
options.feedback: The average of 46 matches none of the three Saturdays. The odd one needs a reason before it joins the average.

items.stem: A file has 10,000 rows, and each row repeats the same 40-character course title. A developer stores the title once in a separate table and points each row to it. Which idea is this?

options.text: Storing a repeated fact once and pointing to it.
options.feedback: This is the same move as shortening a repeating message. The repeat is stored once.

options.text: Sorting the rows by course title.
options.feedback: Sorting changes the order of rows. The title is still stored 10,000 times.
Deleting would lose students. The rows differ even though the title repeats.

options.text: Finding an outlier among the rows.
options.feedback: An outlier is one value that differs from the rest. Here every row holds the same title.
